content: In geometry, the term defect (or deficit) at a vertex of a polyhedron refers to the amount by which the sum of the angles of the faces meeting at that vertex falls short of a full circle (360°). If the sum of these angles exceeds a full circle, as is the case for certain vertices in most non-convex polyhedra, the defect is considered negative. Conversely, in a convex polyhedron, the defects at all vertices are positive. The concept of defect can be extended to higher dimensions. In such cases, it represents the amount by which the sum of the dihedral angles of the cells meeting at a peak falls short of a full circle. According to the Oxford English Dictionary, one definition of defect is the quantity or amount by which anything falls short; in mathematics, a part by which a figure or quantity is wanting or deficient. For example, consider a regular dodecahedron, where three regular pentagons meet at each vertex. The defect at any vertex of this polyhedron is 36° (or π/5 radians), which is equivalent to 1/10 of a full circle. Each angle of the pentagons is 108°, and since three such angles meet at each vertex, the defect is calculated as 360° − (108° + 108° + 108°) = 36°. The sum of the defects at all vertices of the dodecahedron equals two full circles (720° or 4π radians). Importantly, the polyhedron does not need to be convex for this property to hold. A generalization of this principle states that the total defect, expressed in terms of the number of full circles, equals the Euler characteristic of the polyhedron. This is a specific case of the Gauss–Bonnet theorem, which relates the integral of Gaussian curvature to the Euler characteristic. In this context, the Gaussian curvature is concentrated at the vertices, as it is zero on the faces and edges. The Gaussian curvature at a vertex is equal to the defect at that vertex. This relationship can be used to determine the number of vertices (V) of a polyhedron. By summing the angles of all the faces and adding the total defect, the result will include one complete circle for every vertex in the polyhedron. However, it is crucial to use the correct Euler characteristic for the polyhedron in question. A common misconception is that every non-convex polyhedron must have some vertices with negative defects. This is not true, as demonstrated by the following counterexample: Consider a cube where one face is replaced by a square pyramid. This elongated square pyramid is convex, and the defects at all vertices are positive. Now, imagine the same cube, but with the square pyramid inverted into the cube, making the shape non-convex. Despite the non-convexity, the defects at all vertices remain positive.
